title: CI/CD & Release Planning
requirement: Oversee release planning, integration, CI/CD across multi-environment infrastructure.

questions.question: What do CI and CD actually mean, and what do people get wrong about them?
questions.answer: With CI, changes merge to main often and get built and tested automatically, so main stays releasable. Continuous delivery means every build is deployable with one approval, and continuous deployment ships every green build. The usual mistake is calling a build server CI while teams sit on long-lived branches.
questions.keyTakeaway: CI keeps main releasable; CD makes releasing a non-event, not a quarterly project.

questions.question: Walk through the stages of a healthy pipeline for a web service.
questions.answer: Fast feedback first: lint and unit tests on every commit. I build the artifact once, then test that immutable artifact through integration and end-to-end, then staging with smoke tests, then production behind an approval gate.
questions.keyTakeaway: Fast gates first, one artifact promoted through environments, nothing manual before staging.

code.snippet:
stages:
  - lint-unit      # minutes: typecheck, lint, unit tests on every commit
  - build          # one immutable artifact, tagged with the commit sha
  - integration    # contract + API tests against the artifact
  - staging        # auto-deploy, smoke tests, security scans in parallel
  - production     # manual approval or automated canary promotion

questions.question: Trunk-based development or feature branches with pull requests?
questions.answer: I go trunk-based: small changes merge to main behind feature flags within a day or two, so integration pain stays small. Long-lived branches hide semantic clashes no diff shows. Pull requests stay, but small and short-lived.
questions.keyTakeaway: Integrate daily in small slices; hide unfinished work with flags, not branches.

questions.question: Which tests gate the pipeline, and which run elsewhere?
questions.answer: I gate on fast, deterministic layers: unit, contract, and a thin set of critical-path end-to-end tests. A flaky gate trains people to retry instead of read. Slow UI suites run nightly.
questions.keyTakeaway: Gate on fast deterministic tests; run slow breadth out-of-band; fix flakiness like production debt.

questions.question: Compare rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments.
questions.answer: Rolling replaces instances gradually, so versions briefly mix. Blue-green flips to a second environment, so rollback is instant but costs double. Canary sends a small slice of real traffic to the new version first. I'd canary the money paths.
questions.keyTakeaway: Rolling is cheap, blue-green flips back instantly, canary proves with real traffic first.

questions.question: How do you plan a release across dev, staging, and production when three teams contribute?
questions.answer: I freeze content by what passed staging and tag from that commit. Order: backward-compatible migrations first, services tolerating both versions second, cleanup last, so rollback never strands data. One release owner holds the written abort criteria and rollback plan.
questions.keyTakeaway: Release what staging proved; sequence migrations for rollback; one owner, written abort criteria.

questions.question: How do you secure a CI/CD pipeline itself?
questions.answer: I treat the pipeline as production. Credentials are least-privilege, injected per environment from a secret manager, never in the repo or logs. I pin dependencies and base images by digest, and pipeline changes get reviewed like application code.
questions.keyTakeaway: Least-privilege deploy credentials, pinned and scanned supply chain, reviewed pipeline changes.

questions.question: Which delivery metrics do you watch to know the pipeline is healthy?
questions.answer: I watch the DORA four: lead time shows flow, deployment frequency shows batch size, change failure rate shows quality, and time to restore shows resilience. I read them as trends, never as individual scores, or they get gamed.
questions.keyTakeaway: Watch lead time, frequency, failure rate, and restore time as trends, never as blame.

questions.question: How would you design the metrics monitoring and alerting pipeline for a large infrastructure?
questions.answer: Five stages: agents collect metrics, transport ships them, a time-series store persists them, alerting evaluates rules, and dashboards visualize. The load is write-heavy, so a time-series store beats a general database. I roll up data: raw for days, hourly for a year. Alerts get grouped against fatigue, and monitoring runs out-of-band so an outage doesn't take its telemetry down.
questions.keyTakeaway: Collect, ship, store as time series with rollups, alert with grouping, out-of-band from production.

questions.question: How do you keep CI fast in a monorepo where one commit touches dozens of packages?
questions.answer: I build a dependency graph, compute the affected set from the files a commit touches, and run only those packages' jobs, with Nx, Turborepo or Bazel. Remote caching restores anything whose inputs hash the same. The risk is a stale graph skipping affected code, so I keep a nightly full build as a safety net.
questions.keyTakeaway: In a monorepo, build only what the dependency graph says changed; everything else rides the cache.

questions.question: What is your policy for flaky tests in CI?
questions.answer: A flaky gate is worse than no gate, because people just hit retry. Any test that fails without a code change gets quarantined out of the gating job right away, with an auto-filed ticket, an owner, and a one-week fix-or-delete deadline. Retries never pass the gate.
questions.keyTakeaway: Quarantine a flaky test with a tracked ticket and a deadline, or delete it — never normalize retries.

code.snippet:
unit-gate:
  script:
    - pytest tests/ -m "not quarantine"      # flaky tests never gate here
quarantine:
  script:
    - pytest tests/ -m quarantine --maxfail=1
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
# each quarantined test carries an owner and a one-week fix-or-delete ticket

questions.question: Why build once and promote the same artifact through environments?
questions.answer: If staging tests artifact A and production deploys B, the green tests were theater. So I build exactly once, tag it immutably with the commit digest, and every promotion references that digest, never a moving tag like latest. Only injected configuration and secrets differ per environment.
questions.keyTakeaway: Test the digest you deploy; rebuilding anywhere in the chain voids every upstream result.

questions.question: How do you keep staging honest when production is a hundred containers and staging is three?
questions.answer: I think of parity as a budget and spend it on the axes that already bit us: orchestration, service mesh, config mechanism, and database engine. Fewer replicas and smaller data are fine, but topology must not diverge. Config is injected at deploy time, so one artifact runs everywhere. I use synthetic or anonymized data, never full production copies.
questions.keyTakeaway: Staging should be production shrunk, not production simplified; inject config, never bake it.

questions.question: How do you ship a database schema change without taking the table offline?
questions.answer: Expand and contract. First deploy the backward-compatible expansion: a nullable column, a throttled batch backfill, and dual-write if semantics changed. Then ship code that reads and writes the new shape. Only after no old version remains do we drop the old column. Each step is its own release.
questions.keyTakeaway: Expand first, migrate in place, contract last — every deploy step stays reversible.

code.snippet:
pre_deploy:
  script:
    - ./migrate up --target "expand-$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA"   # additive, backward-compatible only
    - ./migrate verify --compatible-with previous-release
deploy:
  script:
    - ./release app --strategy rolling --wait-healthy
# contract steps (drop old column) ride a later release train

questions.question: How do feature flags change the way you release software?
questions.answer: Flags separate deploy from release. Code ships dark, and exposure is a config change that applies and reverts in seconds, faster than a rollback pipeline. I expose gradually: internal users, a percentage, then everyone. The cost is debt, so every flag gets an owner and an expiry ticket at creation.
questions.keyTakeaway: Feature flags turn release into a configuration change, decoupling who sees code from when it deploys.

questions.question: How do you handle deployment freezes and change-approval bureaucracy without killing velocity?
questions.answer: I treat a freeze as a scoped risk decision: name the period, the systems, and an exception lane for customer-impacting fixes and security patches. The pipeline records tests, scans and review as change-control evidence. Routine reversible changes get auto-approved, and risky ones need one sign-off.
questions.keyTakeaway: A freeze is a scoped risk decision with a documented exception lane; tier routine changes by risk, not by meeting.

questions.question: Where do caches actually pay off in a pipeline, and how do you keep them honest?
questions.answer: Dependency caches keyed on the lockfile hash skip reinstalling an unchanged tree, and Docker layer caches rebuild only changed layers. I key on the exact input hash and scope caches per branch. A miss must degrade to a full passing build. The costly failure is a stale cache turning the pipeline green.
questions.keyTakeaway: Cache by exact input hash, scope per branch, and treat a stale-cache green build as a first-class failure mode.

questions.question: How would you automate release notes and versioning instead of hand-writing changelogs?
questions.answer: I derive both from merged history. Conventional commits feed a release tool that computes the semantic version: breaking is major, feature is minor, fix is patch. It drafts notes with linked pull requests. I lint commit messages in CI.
questions.keyTakeaway: Generate versions and notes from merged commits so the changelog describes what actually shipped.

questions.question: When should rollback happen without a human, and how do you automate it safely?
questions.answer: I automate the retreat on objective signals. If error rate, latency or saturation breaches a threshold in an observation window after deploy, the CD system flips traffic back to the last known-good artifact faster than people can convene. The signal must be specific to the new version, with a cooldown against flapping. Humans get paged with evidence.
questions.keyTakeaway: Automate the rollback trigger on objective signals; humans handle the fix, not the retreat.

questions.question: How do you get cloud credentials into CI without long-lived keys?
questions.answer: I federate with OIDC. The CI job requests a short-lived signed token with claims like repository and branch, and the cloud STS exchanges it for credentials scoped to one role and valid for minutes. The IAM policy trusts the exact issuer and subject, so a fork or stolen runner key gets nothing. That removes the static cloud key.
questions.keyTakeaway: Federate CI to clouds with short-lived OIDC tokens; a compromised runner should yield nothing durable.

code.snippet:
permissions:
  id-token: write    # mint OIDC token; no stored cloud keys
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
    with:
      role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/pipeline-deploy
      aws-region: us-east-1

questions.question: What do SBOMs and provenance attestations actually buy you?
questions.answer: An SBOM lists every direct and transitive dependency, so on the next Log4j day you query a database instead of forty repositories. Provenance records how an artifact was built, signed by the build platform. Together they let an admission controller refuse unsigned artifacts at deploy. Generate both inside the build.
questions.keyTakeaway: Sign the artifact with its SBOM and provenance, and enforce verification as a deploy-time gate.

code.snippet:
syft packages -o spdx-json "app:$SHA" > sbom.spdx.json
cosign attest --key "$KMS_KEY" --predicate sbom.spdx.json "app:$SHA"
cosign sign --key "$KMS_KEY" "app:$SHA"
cosign verify-attestation --key "$COSIGN_PUB" "app:$SHA" || exit 1

questions.question: Design the hotfix path from production outage to fix deployed — what can it skip?
questions.answer: Nothing, really. It runs the same gates, just faster. A hotfix branches from the exact production tag, carries a minimal change, and gets queue priority, a trimmed test selection that still covers the blast radius, and a pre-approved expedited sign-off. We never skip the artifact build, migration checks or post-deploy verification.
questions.keyTakeaway: The hotfix lane runs the same gates faster, never fewer.

questions.question: Preview environments per pull request sound great — how do you keep them from bankrupting you?
questions.answer: It's worth it only with a lifecycle owner, because preview namespaces outlive pull requests by weeks. I automate it: create on first push, destroy on merge or close, plus a TTL reaper for orphans. To cut cost I share add-ons, use schemas on a shared database, and run stateless parts on spot capacity.
questions.keyTakeaway: Preview environments win on isolation only if an automated lifecycle reaper wins on cost.

questions.question: CI jobs are queuing for twenty minutes at peak — how do you approach runner capacity?
questions.answer: I measure queue time per stage first, because the cure differs: a morning spike wants warm capacity, a release spike wants per-team limits. Self-hosted runners should be cattle: ephemeral, from a pre-baked image, destroyed after one job. I autoscale on queue depth with a small warm pool.
questions.keyTakeaway: Runners should be ephemeral, pre-baked cattle scaled by queue depth, not hand-maintained pets.

questions.question: Main keeps breaking even though every pull request was green before merge — what is the fix?
questions.answer: Each pull request passed against a main that no longer exists at merge time, so two green changes combined are untested. A merge queue stacks pending pull requests on main's head and runs the gating suite on the combined result before landing. A failure triggers bisection. The cost is some added latency.
questions.keyTakeaway: A merge queue tests pull requests combined against main's head, so main is always exactly what passed.

questions.question: How do you decide a canary is healthy without staring at dashboards?
questions.answer: I formalize it as automated analysis. Define the metrics before rollout: error rate, tail latency, saturation, and a business signal like conversion. Compare the canary against a stable baseline over a fixed window. Flagger or Argo Rollouts step traffic up and promote or abort. A canary nobody analyzes is a slow outage.
questions.keyTakeaway: Let objective canary metrics promote or roll back automatically; humans only choose and tune the metrics.

questions.question: How should infrastructure changes flow through the same CI/CD discipline as application code?
questions.answer: The pipeline is the only door. A pull request runs plan against real state and posts the diff, so reviewers approve a described change. Merge applies it with credentials no human holds. State is remote with locking, drift detection opens tickets, and policy-as-code in CI encodes the checklist humans stop reading.
questions.keyTakeaway: Every infrastructure change flows through plan on the pull request and gated apply on merge — no console changes.

code.snippet:
plan:   # on pull requests — rendered diff posted for review
  script:
    - terraform plan -out=tfplan -detailed-exitcode
  artifacts: [tfplan]
apply:  # on merge — same plan hash, credentials no human holds
  script:
    - terraform apply tfplan
